title: Pseudoinverse
body:
[[Matrix Inverse]] (MATH 1203) sets out when $A^{-1}$ exists: square, non-zero
[[Determinant]], independent columns. It does not answer the obvious next question, which is
**what do you do when none of that holds**. The Moore-Penrose **pseudoinverse** $A^+$ is the
answer, and it exists for every matrix, of every shape, of every rank.

## What it does

$A^+\mathbf{b}$ always returns something sensible, and which sensible thing depends on the system:

| System | $A^+\mathbf{b}$ gives |
|---|---|
| Square, invertible | $A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, the exact solution. $A^+ = A^{-1}$ |
| Overdetermined, inconsistent | the [[Least Squares]] fit, minimising $\|\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}\|$ |
| Underdetermined, many solutions | the solution of smallest $\|\mathbf{x}\|$ |
| Rank deficient, both problems at once | the minimum-norm least squares solution |

That bottom row is the point. When the columns are dependent, least squares has infinitely many
minimisers and $(A^TA)^{-1}$ does not exist; $A^+$ picks the shortest one out of the set, which is
a definite choice and a defensible one. **It is the generalised inverse: right answer when there
is one, best answer when there is not, canonical answer when there are many.**

## Computing it

From the [[Singular Value Decomposition]] $A = U\Sigma V^T$:

$$
A^+ = V\Sigma^+U^T
$$

where $\Sigma^+$ transposes $\Sigma$ and **inverts each non-zero singular value, leaving the zeros
alone**. That last clause is the whole definition and the reason the SVD is the tool for the job:
inverting a stretch by $\sigma$ is a stretch by $1/\sigma$, and a direction that was collapsed to
zero cannot be un-collapsed, so it is left at zero rather than divided by.

In practice "non-zero" means "above a tolerance". Tiny singular values are numerical noise, and
inverting one multiplies that noise by an enormous number. Truncating them is the standard fix and
is the same idea as [[Low-Rank Approximation]] used defensively.

When $A$ has independent columns the formula collapses to the familiar one:

$$
A^+ = (A^TA)^{-1}A^T, \qquad AA^+ = P
$$

so **the [[Projection]] matrix is $AA^+$** and least squares is $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^+\mathbf{b}$
in one symbol. The three notes are three views of one object.

## The defining properties

$A^+$ is the unique matrix satisfying all four Penrose conditions:

$$
AA^+A = A, \qquad A^+AA^+ = A^+, \qquad (AA^+)^T = AA^+, \qquad (A^+A)^T = A^+A
$$

The first two say each is a weak inverse of the other; the last two say $AA^+$ and $A^+A$ are
symmetric, hence orthogonal projections (see [[Projection]]) rather than skewed ones. Note what is
**missing**: $AA^+ \neq I$ and $A^+A \neq I$ in general. $AA^+$ projects onto the column space and
$A^+A$ onto the row space, and they only become the identity when those are the whole space, which
is the invertible case.
